craft_claim: Indian aesthetic theory recognizes shanta (serene-contemplative sentiment) as a primary aesthetic experience, giving the taxonomy's 'serene, meditative' aliases of tone-reflective an indigenous Indian theoretical counterpart rather than a purely Western introspection category.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of the American Oriental Society 92(1), 1972, article starting p. 80; doi:10.2307/599651
supporting_evidence.note: A peer-reviewed study devoted to shanta rasa in Sanskrit poetics documents the category and its contested ninth-sentiment status — establishing shanta as a recognized, theoretically elaborated aesthetic category in Indian poetics, debated rather than assumed. Bibliographic caution: the Crossref deposit for this DOI lists four creators (Gerow, Aklujkar, Masson, Patwardhan) and two title strings; byline and title are flagged for re-check (dossier §I), and the article was not read in full.

The classical rasa framework establishes eight primary sentiments with stable emotions, determinants, expressions, and transitory states; shanta's addition as a ninth is the later Abhinavagupta position whose debate Gerow and Aklujkar document. Cross-link claim clm-rasa-emotional-aesthetic.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole work: episodic recollection with present-tense assessment of earlier selves
supporting_evidence.note: Tagore's reminiscence supplies an Indian prose exemplar of the inward evaluative voice — reflection on one's own past conducted at a cultured, measured distance.

counterevidence.note: Shanta's status was disputed even within Sanskrit poetics (the traditional list has eight rasas), and shanta carries a detachment/liberation register (nirveda-vairagya) that can pull toward devotional serenity (tone-reverent) rather than personal introspection; the mapping onto tone-reflective is analogical, not lexical.

scope: Indian aesthetic-theory context for the serene/meditative aliases; a load-bearing cross-cultural engagement for card section 8, not a claim that Indian poetics contains an exact 'reflective tone'.
exceptions: Devotional or meditative-object contexts route shanta toward tone-reverent or tone-philosophical; the reflective reading requires the self as object of the reflection.
